knowledge_points.label: A scaling law is a power law: loss vs resource is a line on log-log axes
knowledge_points.statement: A scaling law is a simple, predictive rule mapping a resource (dataset size n, parameters, compute) to loss; empirically, language-model test loss against dataset size is a straight line on a log-log plot, i.e. a power law, which is what makes tuning on small models and extrapolating to large ones possible.

anchors.quote: scaling laws which are simple, predictive rules for model performance. Old and unpleasant: tune hyperparameters on big models. New (over?) optimism: tune on small models, extrapolate to large ones
First, an empirical observation: Loss and dataset size is linear on a log-log plot ... 'Scale-free' or 'Power law' (For language modeling, from Kaplan+ 2020)
Data scaling laws : simple formula that maps dataset size (n) to error ... Monotonic, logistic-like curves [Hestness+ 2017]
Scaling laws - power law relationships for many factors. These scaling laws hold on many different kind of phenomena! They even hold in non-standard settings [Kaplan+ 2020]
scaling laws are these simple, predictive rules of how to go from small scale model performance and behavior, and to try to extrapolate them up to large scale behavior.
I'm going to tune hyperparameters on those big runs, but that's very wasteful. ... I would like to do all of my optimization at the small scale
log of the data set on x-axis, log of loss on the y-axis, log of parameters on x-axis ... All of them linearize log test loss here.
scaling laws that are basically the equivalent to these in downstream benchmarks. ... In those cases, you expect to see a sigmoid functional form
In general, it's going to be monotone-ish if we tune our hyperparameters well. ... That's the noise floor.
this is a scale-free or power law relationship. ... it means that the error that I have is decaying polynomially.
emergence, where suddenly models might show certain kinds of capabilities because accuracy is a much more discontinuous measure than losses.

misconceptions.belief: A straight line on a log-log plot means loss falls by a fixed amount for each fixed amount of extra data.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Linear in log-log means log L = -a log n + c, i.e. L is proportional to n^-a: every multiplication of data by the same factor multiplies loss by the same factor, so absolute gains shrink as n grows.

predict.q: Loss falls from 4.0 to 2.0 when training data goes from 1M to 10M tokens, and the data law is a straight line on log-log axes. Predict the loss at 100M tokens.
predict.why: Each 10x of data multiplies loss by the same factor (here 0.5), so 2.0 x 0.5 = 1.0. A linear extrapolation (4.0 - 2.0 - 2.0 = 0) is the log-log misreading.
predict.targets_misconception: A straight line on a log-log plot means loss falls by a fixed amount for each fixed amount of extra data.

transfer.q: Two model families on the same log-log axes. Family A: slope -0.3. Family B: slope -0.1 but half of A's loss at 1M tokens. Which family has lower loss at 1B tokens (1000x more data)?
choices: A
B
they tie
cannot tell from slopes
transfer.why: Over 1000x, A's loss falls by 1000^0.3 = 7.9x and B's by 1000^0.1 = 2x. Starting from L and 0.5L, A reaches 0.126L and B 0.25L. A steeper slope overtakes a constant head start once the range is wide enough.

retrieval.q: A data scaling law is a straight line of slope -alpha on log-log axes. By what factor does the loss shrink each time the dataset grows 10x?
retrieval.answer: By 10^(-alpha), the same factor for every 10x (e.g. alpha = 0.1 gives about 0.79).

retrieval.q: The lecture contrasts an 'old and unpleasant' and a 'new' way of setting hyperparameters. What are they?
retrieval.answer: Old: tune hyperparameters on big models. New: tune on small models and extrapolate with a scaling law.

knowledge_points.label: Why power laws: estimation error decays polynomially (mean estimation gives 1/n)
knowledge_points.statement: Power laws appear because estimation error decays polynomially in sample size: estimating a mean from n samples of N(mu, sigma^2) gives E(mu_hat - mu)^2 = sigma^2 / n, so log Error = -log n + 2 log sigma, a line of slope -1 on log-log axes, and any rate 1/n^alpha is likewise a scaling law.

anchors.quote: Q: Why do scaling laws show up? We know error should be monotone. But why is it a power law / linear in log-log? A (?): Estimation error naturally decays polynomially.

Toy example: mean estimation ... Task: estimate the average as ... What's the error? By standard arguments.. ... This is a 'scaling law' ... More generally, any polynomial rate 1/ ... is a scaling law
Theory understanding: similar to generalization bounds: mean estimation example
I want to estimate the mean from a bunch of data. ... That's going to be sigma squared over n.

if you can come up with anything that is essentially 1 over n to the alpha plus some constant, when you plot that on a log-log plot, subtracting out the constant term, you're going to get a scaling log.
These are pure curve fitting exercises. ... why polynomials are arguably a very natural class of scaling laws, but there's no golden rule that these are the only ones.

provenance.filtering_note: The stacked fractions on p17 extract as separate fragments ('σ𝑖 𝑥 𝑖' over '𝑛', '𝜎2' over '𝑛'; listed under dropped in discovered.json); the quote above is the reconstruction mu_hat = sum_i x_i / n and E(mu_hat - mu)^2 = sigma^2 / n. The variance-of-the-mean step is asserted 'by standard arguments', not derived. p6's point that classical sample-complexity bounds are upper bounds, not realized losses, is why the deck works from an exact realized error here. Spoken evidence (16:19): the variance step is justified in one sentence ('each of these guys is Gaussian, and that the mu hat is Gaussian'), still not derived. Spoken evidence (16:40-16:59): the general form is stated as 1/n^α 'plus some constant', with the constant subtracted before the line appears; the slide drops the constant (see irreducible-floor-bends-loglog). Spoken evidence (10:33-11:09, Q&A): asked whether scaling laws can be justified, the professor calls them 'pure curve fitting exercises'; polynomials are 'arguably a very natural class' but there is 'no golden rule', and theory (error-rate decay) and physics (limits) supply candidate forms. So the slide's '(?)' after 'A' is meant seriously.

misconceptions.belief: Noisier data (larger sigma) makes the error decay more slowly with n.
misconceptions.why_wrong: sigma enters as the additive term 2 log sigma, a vertical offset; the slope on log-log axes is -1 for any sigma. Noise raises the whole line, it does not tilt it.

predict.q: Two mean-estimation problems, sigma = 1 and sigma = 3. Both go from n = 100 to n = 10,000 samples. By what factor does the expected squared error fall in each?
predict.answer: 100x in both (error = sigma^2 / n; n grew 100x; sigma only sets the offset).
predict.why: log Error = -log n + 2 log sigma: changing n moves along a slope of -1 regardless of sigma, so both lines drop by the same two decades.
predict.targets_misconception: Noisier data (larger sigma) makes the error decay more slowly with n.

transfer.q: A different estimator has error proportional to 1/sqrt(n) instead of 1/n. What is its slope on log-log axes, and how much more data does it need to cut error by 10x?
transfer.why: Error = n^-alpha is a line of slope -alpha; to reduce error by factor k you need k^(1/alpha) times the data.

check.q: Two estimators both have error proportional to σ²/n^(1/2), one with σ = 1 and one with σ = 4. For the σ = 4 estimator, by what factor must n grow to cut its error by 5x?
check.why: Error ∝ n^(−1/2), so a k-fold cut needs k^(1/α) = 5² = 25 times the data. σ only sets the offset, so the factor is 25 for both estimators.
check.varies: the rate exponent (1/2), the target cut (5x) and a noisier σ
check.invariant: error = n^(−α) times a constant: the slope sets the data factor k^(1/α); σ shifts the line without changing it
check.targets_misconception: Noisier data (larger sigma) makes the error decay more slowly with n.

retrieval.q: For estimating a mean from n samples with variance sigma^2, what is the expected squared error, and what line does it give on log-log axes?
retrieval.answer: sigma^2 / n; log Error = -log n + 2 log sigma, slope -1.

retrieval.q: An estimator's error decays as 1/sqrt(n). What slope does that give on log-log axes, and what does the lecture say about any rate of the form 1/n^alpha?
retrieval.answer: -1/2; any 1/n^alpha rate is likewise a scaling law (a power law).

knowledge_points.label: Shallow neural exponents: nonparametric learning scales as n^(-1/d)
knowledge_points.statement: Classical parametric estimators give slope -1 (Error ~ 1/n) but measured neural scaling slopes are far shallower; a nonparametric estimator that bins d-dimensional inputs into boxes achieves Error ~ n^(-1/d), slope -1/d, which motivates, without proving, the view that the exponent reflects the data's intrinsic dimension.

anchors.quote: Fact: Similar arguments show most 'classical' models (regression, etc) have scaling ... This means we should see y = ... What do we find in neural scaling laws? ... Machine translation ... Speech ... Language modeling ... Very different from predictions.. Why might this be?

uniform in 2D unit box ... Approach: cut up the 2D space into boxes with length ... Informally, we have ... boxes, each box gets ... samples ... -dimensions, this becomes ... This means scaling is ... Takeaway: flexible 'nonparametric' learning has dimension dependent scaling laws.

Some have made the following argument (Bahri 2021) ... 1. Scaling laws arise due to polynomial rates of learning ... 2. Some argue the slope ... is closely connected to the intrinsic dimensionality of the data. ... But estimators of intrinsic dimension are sketchy, and this is not airtight..
essentially all the classical models you are expected to have a 1 over n scaling. ... we should expect to see roughly a slope of minus 1
If we fit our neural scaling laws, we will find that our exponents are quite different. ... They're about -0.1, -0.3, -0.1, roughly speaking.
cut it up into little 2D boxes of length n to the negative 1 to the fourth. ... I'll have square root n boxes. ... Each box is going to get square root n samples.
the neural networks I was showing you in these slides are behaving kind of non-parametric regressors in 10 dimensions
I don't quite how much I truly, truly buy this argument. ... There's some of the evidence that might be a little sketchy. ... It relies on estimators of intrinsic dimension

provenance.filtering_note: The measured exponents for MT, speech and LM on p18 are a Hestness 2017 figure; no number is in the text. p19's derivation is 'informal' and partly lost in extraction: the slide prints n^(-1/4) as '𝑛 −4' with the 1 above, and 'we have sqrt(n) boxes, each box gets sqrt(n) samples' as '𝑛 boxes, each box gets 𝑛 samples' with the roots lost; the reconstruction is (n^(1/4))^2 = sqrt(n) boxes, n / sqrt(n) = sqrt(n) samples each, mean error per box ~ 1 / sqrt(n) = n^(-1/2) = n^(-1/d) for d = 2, plus 'other smoothness terms'. The deck does not say what intrinsic dimension a language task would have. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above ('no number is in the text'): the p18 exponents are read aloud as 'about -0.1, -0.3, -0.1, roughly speaking' (17:46), and he attributes the two left panels to Hestness and the right (language-modeling) panel to Kaplan (17:39), not all three to Hestness; the attribution is figure-only and unverified here. The reconstruction of p19 is confirmed aloud: boxes of side n^(-1/4), 'square root n boxes', 'square root n samples' each, error 'roughly 1 over square root of n' (18:40-18:58). Spoken evidence, which corrects 'the deck does not say what intrinsic dimension a language task would have': a slope of -0.1 means the networks behave like 'non-parametric regressors in 10 dimensions' (19:25-19:41), the reading the transfer prompt asks for. He is openly sceptical of the stronger Bahri argument ('I don't quite how much I truly, truly buy this argument', 20:07). The caption spells the authors 'Hestenes' and 'Bari'. Author note (2026-10-02, worked-steps pass): the slide's n^(-1/d) is the bias-only rate of the box estimator; balancing bias (box side h) against variance (1/(n h^d)) in squared error gives the standard n^(-2/(d+2)), which equals n^(-1/d) only at d = 2. Either way the exponent shrinks as d grows, which is the point the slide uses; the prompts follow the slide's n^(-1/d). Slide image audit: p18's image prints the fits, ε(m) = 3.87 m^-0.13 (machine translation), 0.95 m^-0.30 and 1.36 m^-0.30 (speech, DS2 and attention), and L = (D/5.4e13)^-0.095 (language modeling, Kaplan's form), so the spoken 'about -0.1, -0.3, -0.1' matches the slide. p20 (Bahri 2021) plots 4/α_D against dimension with 4/α_D and 2/α_D reference lines; d ≈ 10 for slope 0.1 comes from p19's 1/d, not from p20, whose 4/α_D line would give about 40. misconceptions.belief: A shallower slope than -1 means the neural network is a worse learner than linear regression.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The shallow slope is the price of flexibility: a nonparametric learner that can fit an arbitrary f must spread its samples over n^(1/2) (or more) local regions, so its rate depends on the dimension of the problem, not on a defect of the model.

predict.q: A box-binning nonparametric estimator on inputs of intrinsic dimension d = 4 gets 16x more data. By what factor does its error fall?
predict.why: Error ~ n^(-1/d) = n^(-1/4); 16^(1/4) = 2. The classical rate would give 16x, which is the slope -1 expectation the slide says neural laws violate.
predict.targets_misconception: A shallower slope than -1 means the neural network is a worse learner than linear regression.

transfer.q: You measure a data-scaling slope of -0.1 for a language task. Under the box-estimator reading of slide 19 (slope -1/d), which the professor applies aloud, what effective dimension does that suggest, and what does slide 20 say about trusting that number?
transfer.answer: d ~ 10 (slope -1/d); the slide warns that intrinsic-dimension estimators are 'sketchy' and the argument is 'not airtight'.
transfer.why: The exponent-dimension link is a plausible mechanism, not a measurement; the deck uses it to explain why slopes are shallow, not to compute d. The two slides do not even agree on the constant: slide 20's Bahri plot uses 4/α_D ≈ d, under which a slope of 0.1 would mean d ≈ 40, not 10.

check.q: A box-binning nonparametric estimator has error ∝ n^(−1/d). On inputs of intrinsic dimension d = 6, by what factor must n grow to cut the error by 2x?
check.why: Slope −1/6, so halving error needs 2^6 = 64 times the data. Higher intrinsic dimension means a shallower slope and a much larger data factor for the same gain.
check.varies: direction (dimension given, data factor asked) and d = 6
check.invariant: error ∝ n^(−1/d): the slope is −1/d and a k-fold cut needs k^d times the data

knowledge_points.label: Data composition moves the offset of a data law, not its slope
knowledge_points.statement: Changing the dataset composition (a distribution shift) changes a data scaling law's offset but not its slope, so the ranking of data sources made at small scale persists at large scale; in practice fitting laws per mixture is hard and simply taking the best small-scale dataset works.

anchors.quote: Related question: how does dataset composition affect performance. A: Data composition affects the offset, not the slope. These 'distribution shift' scaling laws can tell us about the importance of collecting diverse data! [Hashimoto 2021]
In practice: data mixture selection via scaling is hard. Natural idea - build data scaling laws. Empirical eval - just take the best small dataset
Picking optimal data mixture using small scale models. Deciding whether to repeat data or not. Combing the two and balancing quality with repetition rate

data set composition for many models really affect the offset of these scaling laws, but their slopes are actually determined by the model class. ... So the slopes might remain the same, and only the intercepts might change.
If you get only one kind of data, it's the errors are high no matter what. ... having more data diversity is very helpful.
you can train really small models on a really small amount of data. ... which one will be optimal if I keep scaling it out to my full training run.
reality is a lot more noisy than this ideal world would suggest. ... You pick the best data mix from the small model, and you just scale that guy up, no scaling law required.
that's consistent with the argument that the intercepts differ, but the slopes don't change. ... the best mixture at small scale is also the best mixture at large scale.
very, very often your slopes don't change. ... Often, the interventions that you do just change the intercept of the scaling laws.

provenance.filtering_note: The parallel-lines plot attributed to Hashimoto 2021 and the mixture-selection comparison on p23 are figures with no numbers in the text layer. The slide does not state under what conditions the offset-only claim fails; p21's three questions are a menu, of which p22-p23 treat mixture and p24/p26 treat repetition. Spoken evidence (22:35-22:57): the reason is given: read as empirical generalization bounds, data laws have slopes 'determined by the model class' and intercepts set by the distribution; he hedges with 'for many models', which is as close as the lecture comes to saying when the claim fails. Spoken evidence (23:00-23:22): the Hashimoto toy model is a linear regression with two sources, where one source alone keeps the error high, so the intercept rewards diversity. Spoken evidence (23:38-25:20): the 'natural idea' on p23 is narrated as data-mixing laws (fit mixture vs loss on small models, extrapolate, pick the minimum); in practice 'reality is a lot more noisy', and the DataDecide study found that picking the best small-scale mix works, 'consistent with' equal slopes. Spoken evidence (27:05-27:19, 35:05-35:29): he generalizes the lesson: 'very, very often your slopes don't change', interventions (regularization, ensembling, SGD vs Adam) mostly move the intercept. Considered as a separate spoken KP and folded here: it is this KP's invariant applied to more interventions.

misconceptions.belief: A data source that looks worse at small scale will catch up once the model is large.
misconceptions.why_wrong: If composition only shifts the offset, the two lines are parallel on log-log axes and never cross; the small-scale ranking is the large-scale ranking.

about the same: composition moves only the offset

transfer.why: Fitting a slope per mixture only pays off if slopes differ between mixtures; the deck's claim is that they do not.

retrieval.answer: The small-scale ranking persists at large scale, so the best small-scale dataset stays best.

retrieval.q: What does the lecture say works for data-mixture selection in practice, compared with building per-mixture scaling laws?

knowledge_points.label: Repeated data is worth less: effective data saturates in the repetition count
knowledge_points.statement: When data is finite and must be repeated, repeated tokens count for less than unique ones: effective data D' grows with unique tokens U_D but saturates as repetitions R_D grow past a constant R_D*, so a data filter that is optimal at small compute should loosen as compute grows.

anchors.quote: Scaling laws under data repetition. In practice, we have finite data - how does repeating examples affect scaling? D' = Effective data; Ud = Unique tokens; Rd* = Constant; Rd = Repetition
Data selection scaling and accounting for finiteness. Given that repeated data is less valuable.. Data selection should then be adaptive to scale !
Scaling laws in compute unbounded settings. Important notes: 1. Scaling laws can 'break' if you blindly apply it. 2. Scaling laws are lower bounds so you can always potentially do better
compute is growing, the amount of data that we have is not growing.

Scaling Data- Constrained Language Models ... up to four epochs with standard training recipes, you just don't get hurt at all. ... your realized scaling law, this dark curve is much worse than the projected scaling law if you had fresh data.
write down a modified functional form that's generally predictive of the behavior of this scaling law under repetition.
you can't just keep repeating passes over the data. ... You can't keep making your models bigger. ... you end up reaching for other things, like ensembling your models
we would probably filter very aggressively. ... if you have a lot of compute, then you want to train on more and more stuff because you're going to not want to repeat on this very high-quality data.
your filter has become looser and looser ... the optimal filters turn out to not be fixed at a function of scale.

provenance.filtering_note: The formula itself (D' = U_D + U_D R_D* (1 - exp(-R_D / R_D*))) is in the figure; the text layer carries only the legend. Slide image audit (p24): the image names the paper (title 'Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models' with Muennighoff et al.'s author block), prints D', and annotates the loss curve 'Up to ≈4 epochs repeating is almost as good as new data', 'Rapidly diminishing returns for more repetitions' and 'At ≈40 epochs, repeating is worthless'; its right panel puts the 10^22-FLOP optimum at 6.34B parameters on 242B tokens (loss 2.359) against 8.67B on 178B (2.376) if repeats counted as new. The value of R_D* (about 15.4 in the paper) is not on the slide. p25's two cautions sit between the mixture and repetition slides and apply to both: a fitted law can break when extrapolated blindly, and it is a lower bound (a better recipe can beat it). Spoken evidence, matching p24: the professor names the paper ('Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models', 25:42) and states the threshold: 'up to four epochs with standard training recipes, you just don't get hurt at all', past which the realized law is 'much worse' than the fresh-data projection (25:42-26:02). Spoken evidence (26:14-27:19): p25 is the infinite-compute study (Percy Liang and a co-advised student): with unlimited epochs, repetition and model size both saturate, so they reach for regularization and ensembling, and those interventions move the intercept with 'surprisingly similar' slopes. Spoken evidence (27:19-28:28): p26 is argued aloud: a small-compute lab filters 'very aggressively' because it cannot use the whole internet anyway, a large-compute lab must loosen the filter rather than repeat the high-quality slice. Spoken evidence (29:22-29:44, Q&A): the p25 plot's x-axis is log-scaled (doubling) despite looking linear, and the y-range is narrow enough that linear and log look the same.

misconceptions.belief: A repeated token is worth as much as a fresh one at any repetition count: 40 epochs over 1B unique tokens is as good as 40B fresh tokens.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective data saturates in R_D: each additional repeat adds less than a fresh token, and past R_D* the increments go to zero. The first few epochs are nearly free (p24: 'Up to ≈4 epochs repeating is almost as good as new data'; the professor, 25:42: 'up to four epochs with standard training recipes, you just don't get hurt at all'), which is why the belief feels right; it fails at many repetitions, where 40 epochs are worth a small fraction of 40B fresh tokens.

predict.q: Hold unique tokens U_D fixed and keep adding epochs. How does the effective data D' gained from each additional epoch change as the epoch count grows? Answer up, down or same.
predict.answer: down: each extra epoch adds less effective data than the one before, so D' rises at first and then saturates toward a ceiling set by U_D and R_D*.
predict.why: The repetition term saturates (exponential in -R_D / R_D*), so D' is bounded, unlike the linear count of tokens seen.
predict.targets_misconception: A repeated token is worth as much as a fresh one at any repetition count: 40 epochs over 1B unique tokens is as good as 40B fresh tokens.

transfer.q: A strict quality filter keeps 10% of a corpus and wins at a small compute budget. The budget grows 100x. Per slide 26, what happens to the best filter strictness and why?
transfer.answer: Loosen the filter: the small kept set would have to be repeated many times, and repeated data is worth less than lower-quality unique data, so the optimum shifts toward more unique tokens.
transfer.why: This is what 'data selection should be adaptive to scale' means: the value of a repeated high-quality token falls while the value of an unseen mediocre token does not.

check.q: A lab has a fixed corpus and a quality filter tuned for its current compute. Its compute budget then shrinks 10x, so it needs far fewer training tokens. Per slide 26, which way should the strictness of the best filter move? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: up: with fewer tokens needed, a smaller high-quality set needs fewer repetitions, so a stricter filter wins
check.why: Repeated tokens are worth less than unique ones. A small budget can be met by the top-quality slice with few repeats, so the optimum moves toward stricter filtering; a large budget forces loosening (data selection should be adaptive to scale).
check.varies: direction of the compute change (shrinks instead of grows)
check.invariant: effective data saturates with repetitions, so the best filter depends on how many tokens the budget needs
check.targets_misconception: A repeated token is worth as much as a fresh one at any repetition count: 40 epochs over 1B unique tokens is as good as 40B fresh tokens.

retrieval.q: In the data-repetition law, what happens to effective data D' as the number of repetitions R_D grows well past the constant R_D*?
retrieval.answer: It saturates: further repeats of the same unique tokens U_D add almost no effective data.

retrieval.q: Why does the professor say data selection should be adaptive to scale?
retrieval.answer: Because repeated data is less valuable, so as compute grows the filter should keep more (lower-quality) unique data rather than repeat a small high-quality set.

knowledge_points.label: The scaling-law design procedure: small models, fit, extrapolate, choose
knowledge_points.statement: To make a design decision for a big model: train a few small models varying the choice, fit a scaling law per option, and pick the option whose law predicts best at the target scale, with the cautions that laws can break when applied blindly, that they are lower bounds, and that downstream metrics scale less predictably than loss.

anchors.quote: The effect of hyperparameters on big LMs can be predicted before training! ... The scaling law based design procedure. ... 1. Train a few smaller models ... 2. Establish a scaling law (e.g. ADAM vs SGD scaling law) ... 3. Select optimal hyperparam based on the scaling law prediction.
How should we allocate our limited resources? Train models longer vs train bigger models? Collect more data vs get more GPUs? Scaling laws provide a simple procedure to answer these.
1. Scaling laws can 'break' if you blindly apply it 2. Scaling laws are lower bounds so you can always potentially do better
Caution - scaling behaviors can differ downstream. Thus far: scaling is predictable and depends mainly on parameters. Catch: downstream scaling can often be much less predictable. Tay et al 2023
Wide or deep? How many heads? Which nonlinearity? We could cargo cult things from existing LMs... but how do these get optimized in the first place?
it's very scary to run these things on a run that is basically, potentially millions of dollars in cost
You can't just copy the choices of others and get something that's better than the state of the art.

If you only have a tiny slice of a compute range, it's very, very difficult to tell if something is scaling polynomially or if something's scaling exponentially. ... Everything looks linear if you zoom in enough.
Turns out NL12 is not your best model. ... It was actually NL32XL, which was a much worse model in perplexity.
scaling laws, generally speaking, are objects that you want to apply on the perplexity side. ... But transfer from perplexity to downstream is a lot less certain than it might initially seem.
before you do your big training run, you should have a rough idea of what you're going to see. ... if the fit is good enough, I'm going to have some confidence that the gap will persist
those are singletons. ... perplexities are very, very clean. ... if you're doing something learning rate or critical batch size scaling laws, you will see some truly horrendous stuff.
let's start with the low variance measurement and then establish scaling regularity there
scaling laws are lower bounds in some sense. ... if I continue this recipe and I scale it up, then this is what I will get. ... So you want to be as close to the proper full run as possible.

provenance.filtering_note: 'A few smaller models' is never quantified; the deck gives no rule for how many sizes, how wide a range, or how many orders of magnitude of extrapolation are safe. p41's downstream unpredictability is one Tay et al. 2023 figure. The opening scenario (p2: ten thousand B200s for a month, 'which model??') is the budget the procedure is meant to serve; converting it to a FLOP budget uses lecture 2's napkin math. Spoken evidence (52:39-53:33): the procedure is stated as a prediction: 'you should be able to actually predict fairly precisely the numerical values' of the big run, and 'if the fit is good enough', you trust 'that the gap will persist'. The number of small models is still not quantified, but the variance question is answered in Q&A (53:43-54:41): each point is usually a single run, because perplexity reruns differ 'in the second decimal place', while learning-rate and critical-batch scaling laws are 'truly horrendous' and get too little variance reduction. Spoken evidence (54:43-55:48, Q&A): downstream laws have the same problem as p41, so establish regularity on a low-variance metric first and argue transfer separately. The p41 figure is read aloud: NL12 has the best perplexity but NL32XL is the better downstream model, 'one of the worst correlations' he has seen (51:39-51:55). Spoken evidence (29:52-30:10), a caution the slides lack: over 'a tiny slice of a compute range' polynomial and exponential growth are hard to tell apart ('Everything looks linear if you zoom in enough'). Spoken evidence (1:10:29-1:10:54): 'lower bounds' means 'if I continue this recipe and I scale it up, then this is what I will get', so a mis-tuned recipe gives a bad law, and the small runs should be 'as close to the proper full run as possible'.

external_prerequisites.note: Turning '10,000 B200s for a month' into a FLOP budget to extrapolate to.

misconceptions.belief: Copying the hyperparameters of a published large model is as good as fitting a scaling law for your own setup.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Slide 3 calls this cargo-culting: those settings were themselves chosen by someone's small-scale study for their data and budget; the procedure exists so you can re-derive them for yours.

misconceptions.belief: A law fit on upstream loss predicts downstream benchmark accuracy equally well.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Slide 41: downstream scaling can be much less predictable than loss.

predict.q: You must choose between two optimizers for a 70B-parameter run. Which option matches slide 42's procedure?
choices: Train both optimizers at 70B once and keep whichever ends lower
Fit a law per optimizer on small runs; pick the better extrapolation
Use whichever optimizer the largest published model was trained with
Tune both on one 100M model and use the winner at 70B unchanged
predict.answer: Fit a law per optimizer on small runs; pick the better extrapolation
distractor_from: 'Use whichever optimizer the largest published model used' <- misconception: 'Copying the hyperparameters of a published large model is as good as fitting a scaling law for your own setup.'
'Tune both on one 100M model' <- plausible: treats one small-scale point as if it were a fitted law (the slide's 'one point is not a law')
'Train both at 70B' <- plausible: skips the small-scale procedure the slide exists to replace
predict.why: Train several small models with each optimizer, fit a law per optimizer, pick the one that extrapolates better to 70B. Steps 1-3 of slide 42. One small model gives a point, not a law, so it cannot say whether the winner stays the winner at scale; copying a published choice is the cargo cult of slide 3.
predict.targets_misconception: Copying the hyperparameters of a published large model is as good as fitting a scaling law for your own setup.

transfer.q: You fit a law on 10M-1B parameter models and extrapolate to 100B. Name the two cautions on slide 25 and the one on slide 41 that bound how much to trust the prediction.
transfer.answer: Laws can break if applied blindly; laws are lower bounds (a better recipe can beat them); downstream scaling can be much less predictable than loss.
transfer.why: The extrapolation is two orders of magnitude beyond the data, the recipe might change at scale, and the quantity you care about may not be the loss you fit.

check.q: A law fit on 10M-1B parameter models predicts a validation loss of 2.10 for a 100B model; the trained 100B model reaches 2.02. Which caution from the deck makes this outcome unsurprising?
choices: Copying a published model's recipe would have matched
Downstream metrics scale less predictably than loss
The fit is invalid, since it missed the target
Laws are lower bounds; a better recipe can beat them
check.answer: Laws are lower bounds; a better recipe can beat them
check.why: Slide 25: scaling laws are lower bounds, so a large run whose recipe improved can land below the predicted loss. The downstream caution (p41) does not apply, since this is the loss itself.
check.varies: an observed outcome (the big model beat its prediction) instead of naming cautions before extrapolating
check.invariant: a fitted law extrapolates one recipe; it bounds what is achievable rather than fixing it
distractor_from: 'Downstream metrics scale less predictably than loss' <- misconception: 'A law fit on upstream loss predicts downstream benchmark accuracy equally well' (misapplied: the quantity here is loss)
'The fit is invalid, since it missed the target' <- plausible: treats any miss as falsification
'Copying a published model's recipe would have matched' <- misconception: 'Copying the hyperparameters of a published large model is as good as fitting a scaling law for your own setup.'

retrieval.q: List the three steps of the scaling-law-based design procedure.
retrieval.answer: 1. Train a few smaller models. 2. Establish a scaling law per option. 3. Select the hyperparameter the law predicts is best at the target scale.

retrieval.q: What does 'scaling laws are lower bounds' mean for a practitioner?
retrieval.answer: The fitted law is what this recipe achieves; a better recipe can do better, so the law bounds, not fixes, attainable loss.

prompts.self_explain: Why does slide 4 call 'tune on small models, extrapolate to large ones' a possible over-optimism?

steps.do: Train a few smaller models for each option (slide 42's example: Adam versus SGD), across a range of sizes.
steps.why: One small model gives a point, not a trend; a law needs several sizes per option.

steps.do: Fit a scaling law per option: loss against model size or compute, a line on log-log axes.
steps.why: Each option's law says how its loss falls with scale, not only where it sits at small scale.

steps.do: Extrapolate each law to the target scale and pick the option predicted to be lower there.
steps.why: Two lines with different slopes can cross, so the small-scale winner is not always the winner at the target; only the fitted slopes show which way it goes.

presentations.notice: listen for: the three steps said as a prediction, and 'confidence that the gap will persist'

knowledge_points.label: Compare architectures and optimizers by their scaling curves, not one big run
knowledge_points.statement: Architecture (Transformer vs LSTM; many architectures in Tay et al. 2022) and optimizer (Adam vs SGD in Hestness 2017) choices are compared by fitting a scaling curve per option at small scale rather than by training a full-size model of each, which reveals whether an option's advantage is a constant offset or a different slope.

anchors.quote: Q: Are transformers better than LSTMs? Brute force way: spend tens of millions to train a LSTM GPT-3. Scaling law way: [Kaplan+ 2021]
Many architectures. Cross-architecture scaling in Tay et al 2022.
What about ADAM vs SGD? [Hestness+ 2017] (Note, this is in 2017, so pre-transformers. RHN is recurrent highway nets)
The brute force way to answer this question is to train a big LSTM GPT-3 ... The scaling law way would be to train a bunch of smaller models
This shows LSTMs have definitely different intercept, maybe even different slope than the transformer.
you certainly don't want something where your slopes are worse because that means as you scale up larger and larger, your models will eventually do worse.
things like performer, which is an efficient attention, that doesn't scale very well. ... The things that we implement are the gated linear unit.
If it doesn't show up in the scaling law, it's not a good intervention.
the intercepts are different, but the slopes are very similar. ... It's rare to get different slopes, even with an intervention as big as SGD to ADAM.

provenance.filtering_note: All three comparisons are figures. Slide image audit (p32): the Adam vs SGD figure prints both fits, SGD ε(m) = 5.37 m^-0.094 and Adam ε(m) = 5.25 m^-0.095 (depth-10 recurrent highway networks), so the slide itself shows the same slope with a constant offset of about 2%; the p30 and p31 figures print no exponents. 'Kaplan+ 2021' on p30 is the 2020 paper. Kaplan's observation that the LSTM gap comes from late-context tokens is in the paper, not the deck. The deck's text does not say whether the Adam vs SGD gap was a slope or offset difference (the p32 fits above answer it). Spoken evidence, agreeing with the p32 fits: 'the intercepts are different, but the slopes are very similar' (35:05), 'rare to get different slopes, even with an intervention as big as SGD to ADAM' (35:19). The transfer prompt still asks the learner to reason about both cases. Spoken evidence (32:19-32:58): the LSTM gap is read as 'definitely different intercept, maybe even different slope', and a worse slope is the case to avoid because the gap grows with scale. Spoken evidence (33:08-34:47): the p31 figure (Tay et al., spelled 'Ek' in the caption) is read aloud: Performer 'doesn't scale very well', GLU is better 'throughout', Switch Transformer scales well, mixture of softmaxes looks effective but is unused. The lesson drawn is that small-scale trends anticipated today's frontier choices, hence the slogan 'if it doesn't show up in the scaling law, it's not a good intervention' (34:31).

prerequisites.note: These are instances of step 2 ('establish a scaling law per option').

misconceptions.belief: If option A beats option B at 100M parameters, A beats B at every scale.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only if the two laws are parallel (a pure offset). Laws with different slopes cross, and a comparison at one size cannot tell the two cases apart; several sizes can.

predict.q: On log-log axes, at 10M parameters the LSTM is 0.1 worse in log-loss than the Transformer; at 100M it is 0.2 worse. At 1B, does the gap widen, stay about 0.2, or shrink? (answer widens / same / shrinks)
predict.answer: widens: about 0.3 if the trend holds; the lines have different slopes, so this is not a constant offset.
predict.why: A gap that grows per decade means different exponents; extrapolating the two lines separately shows the Transformer pulling away. A fixed-offset reading would predict 0.2 again.
predict.targets_misconception: If option A beats option B at 100M parameters, A beats B at every scale.

transfer.q: Optimizer P and Q give parallel lines on log-log loss-vs-parameters with P 5% lower. Optimizer R has a steeper slope than P but higher loss at every small size you ran. Which comparison can be settled without extrapolation and which cannot?
transfer.answer: P vs Q is settled at any size (parallel lines never cross: P wins everywhere). P vs R cannot be: a steeper line crosses P's eventually, so you must extrapolate both to the target size and see which side of the crossing it lies on.
transfer.why: This is why the procedure fits a law per option rather than ranking at one scale: the law carries the slope, and the slope decides crossings.

check.q: On log-log axes, option A follows log10(loss) = 0.8 − 0.05·log10(N) and option B follows log10(loss) = 1.25 − 0.10·log10(N), with N in parameters; at N = 100M, B has the higher loss. At what N do the two lines cross? Give N in billions of parameters.
check.why: Set 0.8 − 0.05x = 1.25 − 0.10x: 0.05x = 0.45, x = 9, so N = 10^9 = 1B. Below 1B option A wins; above it the steeper B wins, so a ranking at 100M does not hold at every scale.
check.varies: explicit fitted lines instead of a verbal description, and the crossing point is computed
check.invariant: lines with different slopes on log-log axes cross; only parallel lines preserve the ranking at every scale
check.targets_misconception: If option A beats option B at 100M parameters, A beats B at every scale.

retrieval.answer: Brute force: spend tens of millions training an LSTM GPT-3. Scaling-law way: compare the two families' loss-vs-parameter curves at small scale (Kaplan 2020).

knowledge_points.label: Shape matters little past 2 layers; embedding parameters are not like the rest
knowledge_points.statement: Within Transformers, going from 1 to 2 layers matters a lot but more depth has diminishing returns below about 10^7 parameters and aspect ratio is broadly insensitive, so parameter count dominates shape; however not all parameters are equal: embedding parameters do not scale like the rest (Kaplan counts non-embedding parameters), and mixtures of experts change the value of a parameter.

anchors.quote: Does depth or width make a huge difference? 1 vs 2 layers makes a huge difference. More layers have diminishing returns below 10^7 params
Depth/Width: and other Transformer hypers. Do hyperparameters like the aspect ratio depend on scale?
We've been thinking about 'parameters' but not all parameters are equal. Embedding layer parameters don't behave the same! Related: recent papers on scaling laws for mixtures of experts.
Side note - 'Value of parameters'. With MoEs, we expect parameter scaling to change
having extremely few layers is very, very bad for your model. ... If you have one layer, you're not going anywhere. ... Greater than 1 layer, actually, it's surprisingly more competitive
at different model sizes, we get basically the same minima around 100d model for every layer, or maybe a little bit less.
not all parameters are created equal. ... your scaling laws may look good or bad depending on how you define what a parameter is.
if they drew their scaling laws for depth with the embedding parameters, they got these very funky-looking scaling laws ... they were only going to count the non-embedding parameters
scaling laws and all these kinds of predictability across scales is engineered. ... They don't happen automatically.
scaling trends as a function of both parameters and active parameters. ... you're going to end up with more sparse and sparse models.
the parameters in an MoE that are not active are still helping you reduce your loss

provenance.filtering_note: '107 params' in the text layer is 10^7 with the superscript lost. The aspect-ratio insensitivity on p34 is a Kaplan figure; the text layer only asks the question. Slide image audit (p34): the image includes Kaplan's Figure 5 caption: performance 'depends very mildly on model shape' at fixed non-embedding N, the aspect ratio 'can vary by a factor of 40 while only slightly impacting performance', (n_layer, d_model) = (6, 4288) is within 3% of the (48, 1600) model, and '22% additional compute compensates for 1% loss increase'. p35's embedding claim is Kaplan's Figure 6 (loss vs total vs non-embedding parameters), shown not stated numerically. How MoE parameters should be counted (active vs total) is not specified; p36 is a side note with no citation in the text layer. Slide image audit (p36): the image names the paper (Abnar et al., Apple/MIT, 'Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models') and plots pretraining loss against both total and active parameters, coloured by sparsity, with an IsoFLOP surface over sparsity and active parameters. Spoken evidence (35:58-36:21): one layer is 'a terrible, terrible scaling trend'; beyond one layer models are 'surprisingly more competitive', though more layers are better at every compute level in this figure. Spoken evidence on p34: the Kaplan figure is read aloud: the same minimum 'around 100d model for every layer, or maybe a little bit less' at every size, with a slight drift (36:45-37:07); the argument for sweeping the aspect ratio is the spoken KP scale-invariant-hyperparameters. Spoken evidence (37:55-38:23): Kaplan saw 'funky-looking' laws with embedding parameters included and dropped them on the grounds that the rest 'are doing computation'; this has 'non-trivial implications' later (kaplan-chinchilla-discrepancy). He adds Percy Liang's point that predictable scaling 'is engineered' by choosing the x-axis and setting hyperparameters right (38:28-38:53). Spoken evidence, which corrects 'how MoE parameters should be counted ... is not specified' (39:24-40:46): the Apple/MIT study (Abnar et al. 2025, cited on p55) plots loss against both total and active parameters; the loss-minimizing model becomes sparser as total parameters grow, and at fixed active parameters (fixed compute) more total parameters still lower the loss; he skips the functional form (40:46). Not made a KP here: lecture_04 owns 'more parameters at the same FLOPs'. Spoken slip (35:38-35:52): 'in lecture 2, I told you about aspect ratios ... It's like four times the reasonable multiplier': the architecture lecture is lecture 3, 4x is the d_ff/d_model multiplier, and that lecture's aspect ratios are about 100-200 (lecture_03 aspect-ratio). Not imported.

knowledge_points.label: Critical batch size: the steps-vs-examples trade and its balanced point
knowledge_points.statement: For a target loss, sweeping batch size trades optimizer steps S against examples E along a curve with asymptotes S_min and E_min; the critical batch is the balanced point, costing roughly 2x the minimum steps and 2x the minimum examples, it is claimed to be close to the gradient noise scale (trace of the gradient covariance over the squared gradient norm), and it grows as the target loss gets smaller.

anchors.quote: Batch size - known to have strong diminishing returns past a certain point. Critical batch = min number of examples before diminishing returns (what does that mean?)

Pick a target loss and train 1). Steps needed (S), 2). Examples needed. ... Sweep over batches ... The curve should follow roughly.. ... Fit for ... on this curve and pick ... This balances both sides of the equation, giving roughly 2x the steps / passes optimal
(this is claimed to be close to the ratio of the trace of the gradient covariance and squared norm of the gradient)
Batch size: critical batch size. The smaller the loss target, The bigger the batch

anchors.ref: arXiv:1812.06162 eq. 2.11 and the noise scale B_noise

anchors.quote: two things that you really do have to maybe reinvent in some sense is the batch size and the learning rate. ... You change one, you have to change the other.
a big batch size gives us opportunity for parallelization. ... Remember, data parallel requires large batch size.
I might call this the noise-limited regime. ... every additional element that you throw in your batch reduces the gradient noise in your SGD step.
You're now bias-limited. ... there's always a disagreement between my local descent direction and where the global optimum is.
the goal now should be to balance these two sides. ... the critical batch size is the minimum number of examples that I need divided by the minimum number of steps that I need.
It's going to give me a little bit more number of steps than optimal. ... It's going to require a little bit more examples than optimal
You can do this by just looking at the ratio of the gradient covariance in the squared norm of your gradient.
as you go down in scale in the loss, so your loss is improving, the amount of critical batch size increases. ... once again, a power law.
As you get closer and closer and closer to the minimum, the value of variance reduction increases.

misconceptions.belief: Doubling the batch size always halves the number of steps to reach a target loss.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only well below the critical batch. Past it, steps stop falling (they approach S_min) while the examples consumed keep rising; that is the 'strong diminishing returns' of slide 37.

predict.q: For a target loss you fit S_min = 10,000 steps (huge-batch limit) and E_min = 10M examples (tiny-batch limit). At the balanced critical point of slide 38, roughly how many steps and how many examples does training take?
predict.why: The balanced point of the steps-examples curve costs roughly 2x the minimum of each; you cannot get S_min and E_min at the same time.
predict.targets_misconception: Doubling the batch size always halves the number of steps to reach a target loss.

choices: A
B
same
cannot tell

retrieval.q: Define the critical batch size in words.
retrieval.answer: The minimum number of examples per batch before diminishing returns set in (the balanced point of the steps-vs-examples trade).

retrieval.q: What quantity is the critical batch claimed to be close to?
retrieval.answer: The ratio of the trace of the gradient covariance to the squared norm of the gradient (the gradient noise scale).

prompts.self_explain: Why would the ratio of gradient noise to gradient signal determine where more examples per step stop helping?

steps.do: Fix a target loss and sweep the batch size B; for each B record the steps S and the examples E = B·S needed to reach it.
steps.why: Each batch size is one way of reaching the same loss, so the sweep traces a trade-off between steps and examples.

steps.do: Fit S_min and E_min to the curve the p38 figure plots.
steps.why: A huge batch approaches S_min steps (no more noise left to average away); a tiny batch approaches E_min examples (no example wasted). Real runs sit between the two asymptotes.

steps.do: Balanced point: make both factors equal, S/S_min − 1 = E/E_min − 1 = 1, so S = 2·S_min and E = 2·E_min.
steps.why: The product is fixed at 1, so the symmetric choice is 1 × 1: the same 2x overhead in steps and in examples, the slide's 'roughly 2x'.

steps.do: With S_min = 10,000 steps and E_min = 10M examples: about 20,000 steps and 20M examples, at B_crit = E_min / S_min = 1,000 examples per step.
steps.why: Below B_crit, a bigger batch mostly saves steps; above it, a bigger batch mostly wastes examples.

presentations.notice: 'set B = B_crit' puts the point at the open circle, 2× S_min steps and 2× E_min examples; far below B_crit doubling the batch nearly halves the steps, at B_crit it saves 25%, and far above it almost none.

knowledge_points.label: Optimal learning rate drifts with scale unless the parametrization is muP
knowledge_points.statement: Under naive scaling the optimal learning rate depends on model scale, so an LR tuned on a small model is wrong on a large one; scale-aware initialization and learning-rate scaling (muP, Yang et al. 2022; Yao et al. 2024) make the optimum transfer across scales.

anchors.quote: Learning rates: muP and scale-aware LR choices. Yang et al 2022, Yao et al 2024. If we naively scale up - optimal learning rate depends on scale. We need scaling aware initialization and learning rate scaling
I'll go into this much more detail in the advanced scaling lecture. ... But learning rates generally shift.
people also rescale the network in various ways. ... in order to force the model to have the same learning rate minimum across scales. ... And this is an idea that is called mu p
Some people have reported great success with these kinds of approaches, others have reported less success.
you can try to estimate what these minima are and try to predict what your minimum will be. ... Or you can reparameterize your model to try to keep the learning rate minimum the same
anecdotally it does seem more people are maybe favoring the scaling law approach, but both are certainly viable approaches.

provenance.filtering_note: One slide. The text layer states no muP rules and no drift direction, and 'Yao et al 2024' has no title or link. Slide image audit (p40): the image carries both. Yang et al. 2022's panels plot training loss against log2 learning rate for widths 128-8192: under 'Standard Practice' the minimum moves to smaller learning rates as width grows ('optimum shifts'), under muP it stays put ('optimum stable'). Yao et al.'s Table 2 ('μP function for a model M′ that is r times the widths of M') gives the rules: AdamW learning rate l → l/r and init variance σ → σ/r for matrix-like weights, output multiplier τ → τ/r, embeddings and other weights unchanged. Spoken evidence, matching the p40 figure: for width scaling under standard parametrization the optimal learning rate goes down, roughly as 1/width (48:59-49:21); this became the spoken KP lr-shrinks-with-width. Spoken evidence (49:32-50:50): muP is described as rescaling initialization sizes and per-part optimizer step sizes 'to force the model to have the same learning rate minimum across scales', with mixed reported success; the p40 figure shows the two philosophies: predict how the minimum moves (it moves 'pretty predictably'), or reparametrize so it stays put. Both have been used in large runs; 'anecdotally' more people favour the scaling-law approach. Details deferred to the advanced scaling lecture (48:36, 50:50).

misconceptions.belief: The best learning rate found on a 100M model is the best learning rate for the 10B model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Under naive (standard) parametrization the optimum moves with scale; only under a scale-aware parametrization like muP does it stay put.

knowledge_points.label: Joint data-model laws: a sum of power laws in n and m
knowledge_points.statement: Joint laws write error as a sum of power laws in data n and model size m: Rosenfeld et al. 2020, Error = n^(-alpha) + m^(-beta) + C, and Kaplan et al. 2020, Error = [m^(-alpha) + n^(-1)]^beta; exponents fit on small data and small models predict the rest of the grid, and the larger term acts as a floor, which is why 'lots of data is wasted on small models'.

anchors.quote: Clearly, lots of data is wasted on small models ... Joint data-model scaling laws describe how the two relate ... From Rosenfeld+ 2020, ... From Kaplan+ 2020 ... Provides surprisingly good fits to model-data joint error.
Model-data joint scaling is accurate ... From Rosenfeld – fit scaling exponents on small data, small models. Predict rest. ... Trading off data size and model size: optimize ... with your costs.
data times the parameters is roughly your FLOPs, linear in that.
if we take a teeny tiny model and we dump tons of data into it, that will just be wasted. ... This is a complete waste of compute.
Kaplan and Rosenfeld both proposed these functional forms, which are roughly equivalent ... Rosenfeld is very simple. ... It's really just the sum of two inverse terms.
If I have an infinite amount of data, then what happens? ... You become a pure model size scaling law. ... take the limits of all the variables to understand the behavior of the system.
you're going to fit on these green points, which is a low compute regime and low data regime. ... you can very accurately predict the error
subject to my FLOPs constraints, minimize this. ... That's a simple nonlinear optimization problem.

provenance.filtering_note: p43's Kaplan form is extracted as '𝐸𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟 = 𝑚−𝛼 + 𝑛−1 𝛽' with the bracket and superscript placement lost; the reconstruction above follows the paper's L(N,D) = [(N_c/N)^(alpha_N/alpha_D) + D_c/D]^alpha_D with constants dropped as on the slide. No fitted exponent values are printed; p44's predicted-vs-actual plot is a figure. The slide says 'optimize with your costs' but gives no cost model; that is what the compute-optimal KPs supply. Spoken evidence, which corrects 'gives no cost model' (57:11-57:30, 59:58-1:00:09): the cost is compute, 'data times the parameters is roughly your FLOPs', and the allocation is the minimization of the joint law 'subject to my FLOPs constraints', 'a simple nonlinear optimization problem'. Spoken evidence (57:32-58:01): the p43 figure is read aloud: the smallest model's curve is flat for a long stretch of data, 'a complete waste of compute'. Spoken evidence (58:52-59:21): the limits are argued: infinite data leaves a pure model-size law, infinite model size a pure data law, with the advice to take the limits of every variable of a proposed law. Spoken evidence (59:21-59:56): p44's fit uses only the small-data, small-model corner and predicts the rest 'very accurately'.

prerequisites.note: Each term is a single-resource power law.

misconceptions.belief: If adding data stops lowering loss, the data has been exhausted or is low quality.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In a sum of power laws the m^-beta term can dominate: the model, not the data, is the bottleneck, and the n term is already negligible.

predict.q: Rosenfeld form with alpha = 0.5, beta = 0.3, C = 0. At n = 10^4, m = 10^4 the error is 0.0100 + 0.0631 = 0.073. You raise n to 10^6 with m fixed. Predict the new error.
predict.why: n^-0.5 drops from 0.0100 to 0.0010 but m^-0.3 = 0.0631 stays; the model term is the floor, so 100x more data buys almost nothing. This is 'data wasted on small models'.
predict.targets_misconception: If adding data stops lowering loss, the data has been exhausted or is low quality.

transfer.q: Same law and starting point (n = m = 10^4). Instead of n, raise m to 10^6 with n fixed. New error, and which term now dominates?
transfer.why: m^-0.3 falls from 0.0631 to 10^-1.8 = 0.0158; adding n^-0.5 = 0.0100 gives 0.0258. The two terms are now comparable, so further gains need both resources.

retrieval.q: Write the Rosenfeld 2020 joint law and name each symbol.
retrieval.answer: Error = n^-alpha + m^-beta + C: n data size, m model size, alpha and beta fitted exponents, C the irreducible error.

retrieval.q: Why is 'lots of data is wasted on small models' a consequence of the additive form of the joint law?
retrieval.answer: The terms add, so whichever is larger floors the error; for a small model m^-beta is large and shrinking n^-alpha further changes nothing.

prompts.self_explain: In a sum of two power-law terms, why does the larger term act as a floor for improvements in the other resource?

steps.do: Rosenfeld et al. 2020: a data term plus a model term plus a constant.
steps.why: Each resource lowers only its own term, so the two can be reasoned about one at a time.

steps.do: Let n → ∞: Error → m^(−β) + C, a pure model-size law.
steps.why: With unlimited data the data term vanishes and the model term is the floor that remains ('take the limits of all the variables').

steps.do: Let m → ∞: Error → n^(−α) + C, a pure data law.
steps.why: Symmetrically, an unlimited model leaves only the data term.

steps.do: Kaplan et al. 2020 has the same limits: m → ∞ leaves n^(−β), and n → ∞ leaves m^(−αβ).
steps.why: The forms differ, but both reduce to single-variable power laws in each limit, which is why the lecture calls them roughly equivalent.
Evaluate each term on its own; the model term is already about six times the data term.

steps.do: Raise n to 10⁶ with m fixed: n^(−0.5) = 0.0010.
steps.why: 100x the data at slope −0.5 divides the data term by 100^0.5 = 10, the same ratio move as in power-law-from-estimation-rate.

steps.do: New error = 0.0010 + 0.0631 = 0.064, only about 12% below 0.073.
steps.why: The model term did not move and was most of the error: this is 'data wasted on small models'.

presentations.notice: When m^−β is much larger than n^−α the blue curve for your model size is already flat on its dashed floor: 100× more data lowers the error by a few percent, while 100× bigger model lowers it by more than half.

knowledge_points.label: Kaplan's allocation: N_opt ~ C^0.73, D_opt ~ C^0.27
knowledge_points.statement: Kaplan et al. 2020 turned the joint law into an allocation rule: for a compute budget C, N_opt grows as C^0.73 and D_opt as C^0.27, so parameters should grow much faster than data and tokens per parameter decrease as C grows.

anchors.quote: 'Optimal' compute and data tradeoffs as a case study. ... Rosenfeld, Kaplan both predict relationship of data, model and perf. ... Kaplan claims: ... 0.73 ... 0.27 (tokens per param decreases w/ C) ... Chinchilla [Hoffman et al] argue these fits are quite off.
Why do we have this big difference? ... Kaplan claims: ... 0.73 ... 0.27 (tokens per param decreases w/ C) ... Why such a big difference (when both fit joint scaling laws?)

The amount of data it should be C to the 0.73, and the amount of model size should be C to the 0.27. ... I think it's reversed, sorry. ... N should be the amount of parameters and D should be the amount of data.
tokens per parameters decreases with C. ... this prescription by Kaplan tells you to train bigger and bigger and bigger models. ... And part of that was driven by this.

misconceptions.why_wrong: 0.27 < 0.73: data grows much more slowly than parameters, so the recommended tokens per parameter fall as compute grows.

knowledge_points.label: Chinchilla's three ways to fit compute-optimal N(C), D(C)
knowledge_points.statement: Hoffmann et al. 2022 estimate compute-optimal N(C) and D(C) three ways: (1) the minimum-loss envelope over the union of all training curves vs FLOPs, (2) IsoFLOPs, where for each fixed FLOP budget the parameter count is varied, the convex loss curve's minimum is taken, and a power law is fit through the minima, and (3) a least-squares joint parametric fit on the size-data grid; methods 1 and 2 agree, and method 3's original fit was flawed until Besiroglu et al. 2024 recovered the data and re-fit it.

anchors.quote: Chinchilla in depth - 3 methods. The chinchilla authors suggest 3 ways of fitting scaling laws - we'll go over each. They mostly (minus method 3) suggest similar constants.
Method 1 - minimum over runs. Similar to the FLOPS figure on Kaplan - the minimum over the union of all training curves is a power law.
Method 2 - IsoFLOPS. Pick a range of FLOP budgets, vary the total parameter count, take the min over these convex shapes. The minima form a power law.
Method 3 - Joint fits. Run a bunch of models on the size-data grid. Use least squares to fit a joint scaling law

Fun addendum - errors in chinchilla method 3. Note that this method three was likely flawed in the original paper. Some authors did data forensics, recovered the raw data, and re-did the fit and got results more consistent with methods 1 and 2 [Besiroglu et al 2024]
Isoflops everywhere. Methods like IsoFLOPS are pretty easy to execute and usually pretty clean. Diffusion - Gulrajani+ 2023. MoEs - Abnar+ 2025.
the Chinchilla author suggests three different ways of fitting scaling laws. ... it's a way of robustifying yourself to modeling assumptions you may have made.
All 1 and 2 both agree that the coefficients for data and for model size are roughly the same. ... 0.5, 0.5, 0.49, 0.51. ... Method 3 does differ, 0.46 and 0.54
for a particular FLOP, this is the best loss that I ever achieved for that FLOP on any training run. ... they should train a 67 billion parameter model.
very tricky defining things like what is the lower envelope
Method 2 is IsoFLOP. ... It's also very easy and very robust. ... This is probably my personal favorite method.
or even fit a quadratic and take the minimum over the quadratics ... These is $63 billion parameters for my compute budget.
how you do the curve fitting is very important. ... This thing also has some trickiness, just like method 1.

Chinchilla method three never agreed with Chinchilla method 1 and 2. ... if you scale up your compute, eventually, actually, in this case, you're going to have way more tokens than you are going to have parameters.

They couldn't get either the raw data or the code. ... they extracted the data from plots in the paper, and they refitted the method 3 regressions. ... the original paper must have underfitted the original data.
Actually, they had made a mistake, and that was the only reason why method 3 disagreed from methods 1 and 2.
IsoFLOP are very easy to execute. ... IsoFLOP is always a good default.

knowledge_points.label: Why Kaplan and Chinchilla disagree: parameter counting and small-scale tuning
knowledge_points.statement: Kaplan's skewed allocation (C^0.73 / C^0.27) and Chinchilla's balanced one differ, although both fit joint laws, because Kaplan counted non-embedding parameters (last-layer parameters removed), and used a warmup too long for the smallest compute budgets (the slide adds that the decay schedule itself is maybe not critical if batch and learning rate are tuned); counting total parameters and accounting for small nonlinearities moves the fit toward Chinchilla.

anchors.quote: Why do we have this big difference? ... Why such a big difference (when both fit joint scaling laws?)
Explanation 1. Kaplan removed last layer param from the count. Warmup at very small compute budgets was too high. (Decay itself is maybe not critical if batch / LR is properly tuned)
Explanation 2. Non-embedding vs total param choice + small nonlinearities
They both did pretty reasonable stuff. ... If you do your own Chinchilla-style analysis, you will find probably scaling is much closer to Chinchilla.
Scaling laws can really change depending on the precise ways in which you're implementing the scaling laws, the hyperparameter settings that you're using, and even what the x-axis is.

Resolving Discrepancy to Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models. ... let's change how we count parameters. ... let's change how learning rate warmup is done. ... let's tune the optimizer a little bit more. ... And then they get exactly the Chinchilla result.

they also excluded the last layer parameter counts, the softmax ones. ... the embedding and the last layer linear are dual to each other. ... whether you include or exclude those has a big material impact on the shape of the scaling law.
a lot of the models that were being trained in Kaplan were very small. ... they were not actually converging by the time that the learning rate warm up was done.
Kaplan et al. was fixing one big batch size, and those big batch sizes were suboptimal for the smaller models.
It's by Pearce and Song. ... they don't train any models. ... They just take the Chinchilla training curves
Kaplan is operating at a much lower compute scale, so they're very sensitive to small changes ... the size of the compute scale plus the slight non-linearity induced by non embedding parameters

Spoken evidence (1:09:07-1:09:40): 'last layer param' is the output (softmax) matrix, dropped with the embedding because the two have the same shape; whether they are included 'has a big material impact on the shape of the scaling law'. knowledge_points.label: A log-log line holds only far from the floor: subtract the irreducible error
knowledge_points.statement: A scaling law is a straight line on log-log axes only while the loss is far above its irreducible floor: with L(n) = E + A·n^(−α), raw log L bends flat as the reducible term A·n^(−α) falls toward E, so its local slope understates α. Laws are therefore fit either inside the power-law regime (for a data law, a model much larger than the data) or by fitting the floor E explicitly and plotting log(L − E).

anchors.quote: it means that the error that I have is decaying polynomially. ... And also, it usually means that I'm very far away from my asymptote. ... Because once I approach my asymptote, I'm going to taper off rather than have a line.
anything that is essentially 1 over n to the alpha plus some constant, when you plot that on a log-log plot, subtracting out the constant term, you're going to get a scaling log.

when the model gets small relative to the data, like you have way more data than you have model size, you enter this irreducible error regime. ... you can't do any better no matter how much data you add.

we usually want to think about this power law regime, which is the simpler case. ... Either that or you explicitly fit the asymptote and then you correct for it. ... usually like 10 times bigger than the data, what have you.
What do we expect out of scaling laws? ... Monotonic, logistic- like curves [Hestness+ 2017]

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (15:33-15:45, 16:40-16:53, and a Q&A answer at 20:39-21:33). Slide p14 shows Hestness's logistic-like curve with an irreducible-error region and p17 says 'any polynomial rate 1/n^α is a scaling law', but no slide says that a straight log-log line is a sign of being far from the floor, that the constant must be subtracted before the line appears, or what to do near the floor. The professor's rule for staying in a data law's power-law regime, a model 'usually like 10 times bigger than the data' (21:21), is quoted but not tested: he gives no units and calls it rough ('what have you'). The local-slope formula (the slope of raw log L is −α·R/(E+R), where R = A·n^(−α), so −α/2 where R equals E) and every number in the prompts are the author's. A model that is too small for its data flattens the curve for a different reason (the model term of a joint law becomes the floor), which joint-data-model-law treats; the transfer prompt asks the learner to tell the two apart.

prerequisites.note: Said in the Q&A that closes the data-scaling theory section (20:39).

misconceptions.belief: The slope of raw log-loss against log-data is the scaling exponent α at every scale.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only far from the floor. With L = E + A·n^(−α), the local slope of log L is −α·R/(E+R), where R = A·n^(−α) is the reducible part, and it flattens toward 0 as R falls toward E. Subtract E first and the line has slope −α.

misconceptions.belief: A data-scaling curve that flattens means the power law has broken and more data is useless.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Flattening is expected near the irreducible floor, or when the model is too small for the data; the reducible part can still follow the same power law. Fit E (or grow the model) and the line comes back.

predict.q: A data law is L(n) = 2.0 + 2.0·(n/n₀)^(−0.5), so the loss is 4.0 at n₀ tokens. Predict the loss at 100·n₀ tokens.
predict.why: The reducible part falls 100^0.5 = 10x, from 2.0 to 0.2, and the floor stays: 2.0 + 0.2 = 2.2. Treating the raw curve as a pure power law with slope −0.5 would give 4.0 / 10 = 0.4, below the floor.
predict.targets_misconception: The slope of raw log-loss against log-data is the scaling exponent α at every scale.

transfer.q: With the model size fixed, your data-scaling curve on log-log axes is straight from 10M to 1B tokens and then flattens out by 10B tokens. Give the two explanations the lecture offers and what you would do about each.
transfer.answer: (1) The model is now small relative to the data and has entered the irreducible-error regime for its model class: rerun with a model much larger than the data to stay in the power-law regime. (2) The loss is approaching the task's irreducible floor: fit L = E + A·n^(−α) and plot log(L − E), which straightens the line.
transfer.why: Both make the raw log-log curve taper; only the second is a property of the task. The professor's two options are to stay in the power-law regime or to 'explicitly fit the asymptote and then correct for it' (21:17).
transfer.targets_misconception: A data-scaling curve that flattens means the power law has broken and more data is useless.
transfer.varies: a measured curve that bends, instead of a formula
transfer.invariant: the power law describes the reducible part of the loss; a floor (task or model) bends the raw curve

check.q: A data law L(n) = E + A·n^(−α) has a known floor E = 2.0. The measured loss is 3.0 at 1B tokens and 2.2 at 10B tokens. What is α?
check.why: Subtract the floor: the reducible part falls from 1.0 to 0.2, a factor of 5 per decade, so α = log10(5) ≈ 0.70. Fitting the raw losses gives log10(3.0 / 2.2) ≈ 0.13, which mistakes the approach to the floor for a shallow exponent.
check.varies: the exponent is recovered from two measurements, and the floor is given
check.invariant: the power law holds for L − E, not for L
check.targets_misconception: The slope of raw log-loss against log-data is the scaling exponent α at every scale.

retrieval.q: With L(n) = E + A·n^(−α), what happens to the local slope of raw log L vs log n as L approaches E, and what does that do to a fitted exponent?
retrieval.answer: It flattens toward 0, so a fit to raw log L understates α.

knowledge_points.label: Sweep shape in scale-invariant units: carry the aspect ratio, not the layer count
knowledge_points.statement: To check a shape hyperparameter across scales, express it as a quantity whose optimum should not move with size: the best number of layers grows as the model grows, but in Kaplan's sweeps the best aspect ratio (d_model per layer) stays roughly the same at every size, so a 'fix the aspect ratio and scale up' recipe is validated by confirming that this minimum does not shift.

anchors.quote: try to identify what you might call scale-invariant quantities, like the aspect ratio. ... The number of layers is not a scale-invariant quantity. ... As you make your model bigger, you do want more layers. ... maybe the aspect ratio, the optimal one should stay the same.
at different model sizes, we get basically the same minima around 100d model for every layer, or maybe a little bit less. ... for the most part, the minima stays roughly similar.
if your scaling strategy is ... I'm going to fix my aspect ratio, and I'm going to scale up ... you can make plots like this and convince yourself we're probably good
Do hyperparameters like the aspect ratio depend on scale?

transfer.q: Your sweeps show the best aspect ratio d_model/n_layer is about the same at every size. Using N ≈ 12·n_layer·d_model², you scale a model up 8x in parameters at that fixed aspect ratio. By what factor does the layer count grow?
transfer.why: With d_model = r·n_layer, N ≈ 12·r²·n_layer³, so 8x parameters means n_layer grows 8^(1/3) = 2x (and d_model 2x as well). Keeping the layer count fixed would put all the growth into width and change the aspect ratio by √8 ≈ 2.8x.
