knowledge_points.label: Wider networks want smaller learning rates: the 1/width rule of thumb
knowledge_points.statement: Under standard parametrization, making a network wider calls for a smaller learning rate, because each step changes more parameters at once; a common rule of thumb scales the learning rate as 1/width, and the alternative to following this moving optimum is to reparametrize (muP) so that it stays put.

anchors.quote: learning rates generally shift. ... I'm only going to do width scaling. ... the bigger my model, the smaller my learning rate should be. ... because I have bigger, more parameters, I'm changing more things at once. ... Maybe I should move less.
there's a rule of thumb that maybe you want to scale by 1 over the width. ... decrease the learning rate regularly as a function of your width
the way in which the minimum changes is pretty predictable, so this is not a crazy idea.
If we naively scale up – optimal learning rate depends on scale.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only for the direction and the rule. Slide p40's text says only that under naive scaling the optimal learning rate 'depends on scale'. Slide image audit (p40): the image shows the direction (under standard practice the optimum moves to smaller learning rates as width grows, 'optimum shifts') and Yao et al.'s muP table, whose matrix-like AdamW learning rate is l/r for an r-times-wider model; the 1/width rule of thumb itself is said aloud, not printed. Aloud (48:42-49:32), for width scaling of a plain MLP: bigger model, smaller learning rate, because 'I'm changing more things at once', and 'a rule of thumb that maybe you want to scale by 1 over the width'. He hedges ('maybe'), sets depth scaling aside ('I'm not going to do depth scaling'), and defers details to the advanced scaling lecture (48:36). He then offers two philosophies (50:08-50:41): predict how the minimum moves ('pretty predictable') or reparametrize with muP so it stays put; anecdotally more people favour the first. The prompts test only the stated 1/width rule. muP's per-layer rules (for Adam, hidden-layer learning rates also scale as 1/fan-in) are printed in p40's table but not narrated, and are not tested here.

prerequisites.note: Batch size and learning rate are introduced together as the two choices to re-tune at scale (41:30).

misconceptions.belief: The learning rate belongs to the optimizer and the data, so changing only the width should not change it.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Under standard parametrization a wider layer applies its per-weight steps to more weights at once, so each step changes the layer's output more; the optimum moves down, roughly as 1/width (48:59-49:21).

misconceptions.belief: A wider model has more capacity, so it can take a larger learning rate.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Capacity is not step size. More weights moving at once makes each step larger in effect, so the lecture's rule goes the other way: smaller learning rate for wider models.

predict.q: You tuned the learning rate to 6e-3 on a width-512 model under standard parametrization. Following the 1/width rule of thumb, what learning rate do you use at width 3072?
predict.why: 3072 / 512 = 6x wider, so the learning rate drops 6x: 6e-3 / 6 = 1e-3. Keeping 6e-3 treats the learning rate as independent of width, which the lecture says it is not under standard parametrization.
predict.targets_misconception: The learning rate belongs to the optimizer and the data, so changing only the width should not change it.

transfer.q: Two runs under standard parametrization use the same learning rate, 3e-3, tuned at width 1024: one at width 1024 and one at width 8192. Which run is more likely to train badly or diverge, and why?
transfer.answer: The width-8192 run. By the 1/width rule its optimum is about 3e-3 / 8 ≈ 4e-4, so it runs at about 8x too high a learning rate; with 8x more weights per layer moving at once, each step changes the layer's output far more.
transfer.why: This is the lecture's reason for shrinking the learning rate with width, applied to a run that skipped it. muP would instead keep 3e-3 valid at both widths by rescaling initialization and per-layer step sizes.
transfer.targets_misconception: A wider model has more capacity, so it can take a larger learning rate.
transfer.varies: a stability judgement about a run that ignored the rule, instead of computing the new learning rate
transfer.invariant: under standard parametrization the optimal learning rate falls as width grows

check.q: Under the 1/width rule of thumb, the learning rate was cut from 4e-3 to 5e-4 when a model was widened. By what factor did the width grow?
check.why: 4e-3 / 5e-4 = 8, and the rule ties the learning rate to 1/width, so the width grew 8x.
check.varies: inverse direction: the learning rates are given and the width factor is asked
check.invariant: optimal learning rate ∝ 1/width under standard parametrization
check.targets_misconception: The learning rate belongs to the optimizer and the data, so changing only the width should not change it.

retrieval.q: Under standard parametrization, which way should the learning rate move when a network is made wider, and what reason does the lecture give?
retrieval.answer: Down: a wider network changes more parameters at once with every step, so each step should move less.

retrieval.q: What rule of thumb does the lecture give for scaling the learning rate with width, and what is the alternative philosophy?
retrieval.answer: Scale the learning rate as 1/width (predict how the optimum moves); or reparametrize with muP so the optimum stays the same across widths.

knowledge_points.label: In one-pass training, train loss stands in for validation loss
knowledge_points.statement: Most pre-training runs see each token once (one-pass SGD), so the generalization gap is very small and training and validation loss are nearly equal; scaling-law plots therefore use them interchangeably, but this breaks once data is repeated (multi-epoch, data-constrained or infinite-compute settings), where held-out loss must be used.

anchors.quote: You fit to test loss when you're doing good scientific practice ... except for a very few, like the infinite compute one and the repetition stuff ... you're doing one-pass SGD.

the generalization gap for all of these models is very, very small. ... So train and val are very similar. ... I've seen some pre-training code bases that don't even have validation loss. ... That's why a lot of these plots exchange those two, because they're all in the one-pass regime.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only, in a Q&A answer (55:50-56:35) to a student who noticed that some plots show test loss and others training loss. No slide mentions the train/validation distinction. The exceptions he names (the infinite-compute and repetition studies) are the multi-epoch settings of data-repetition-effective-data. Why one-pass training loss tracks test loss (each batch is scored before the model has trained on it, so it is a fresh sample from the training distribution) is the author's explanation, not said; so are all numbers in the prompts. 'Kaplan 2021' (55:57) is the 2020 paper, as on p30. The rule says nothing about distribution shift: training loss is not a stand-in for loss on a different evaluation distribution.

prerequisites.note: The exceptions are the repeated-data settings.
Said in the Q&A after the procedure (53:35-56:35).

misconceptions.belief: Training loss is never a valid stand-in for test loss in a scaling study, because models overfit their training data.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Overfitting needs repeated exposure. In one-pass pre-training each token is seen once, so the generalization gap is 'very, very small' (56:15) and training and validation loss nearly coincide.

misconceptions.belief: If training and validation loss match in one-pass runs, they will also match when the same data is repeated for many epochs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Repetition is the exception the professor names: once tokens are seen again the model can fit them specifically, and training loss falls below held-out loss.

predict.q: A 1B-parameter model is trained for one pass over 100B unique tokens, ending with a training loss of 2.31. What do you expect its loss on a held-out split of the same distribution to be?
choices: about 2.31: almost no gap in one pass
about 2.9: overfitting adds a large gap
about 1.8: held-out text is easier
unknowable without a separate eval run
predict.answer: about 2.31: almost no gap in one pass
distractor_from: 'about 2.9: overfitting adds a large gap' <- misconception: 'Training loss is never a valid stand-in for test loss in a scaling study, because models overfit their training data.'
'unknowable without a separate eval run' <- same misconception, in its cautious form
'about 1.8: held-out text is easier' <- plausible: no reason for same-distribution held-out text to be easier
predict.why: Each token is seen once, so the training loss on each batch is measured on data the model has not yet trained on; the generalization gap is very small and the two losses nearly coincide. That is why many scaling plots use either one.
predict.targets_misconception: Training loss is never a valid stand-in for test loss in a scaling study, because models overfit their training data.

transfer.q: You are fitting a data-constrained scaling law in which 5B unique tokens are repeated for 16 epochs. Should you plot training loss as in your one-pass runs? Explain.
transfer.answer: No. With 16 repetitions the model sees each token many times and can fit them, so training loss falls below held-out loss. Use a held-out validation split; the one-pass equivalence holds only when every token is fresh.
transfer.why: The professor's exceptions are exactly the repetition and infinite-compute studies, where epochs are many.
transfer.targets_misconception: If training and validation loss match in one-pass runs, they will also match when the same data is repeated for many epochs.
transfer.varies: a multi-epoch setting instead of a one-pass run
transfer.invariant: train ≈ test loss only while every token is seen once
